commitResults.messageTitle: Refactor main into parser.java and Ui.java
Configure Gradle for the bucket package
Add tests for parser and event classes

commitResults.messageBody:
Turn Ui into a message builder: each show method becomes a get methodthat returns its text rather than printing it. Move the body of thecommand loop into Bucket#getResponse, which runs one line and returnsone reply. The console loop still calls it in a while loop, while theGUI calls it once per button press, which is the only shape anevent-driven front end can use.

Build the GUI with FXML so the layout can be edited in Scene Builderwithout touching Java. Start from Launcher rather than Main, becauseJavaFX refuses to start when the class holding main extendsApplication but its libraries came off the plain classpath

The code carries assumptions that are never stated. Ui only works once
start() has opened its scanner, MainWindow only works once setBucket()
has run, and several methods dereference what they are handed without
checking it. When one of these is broken the symptom is a
NullPointerException somewhere further on, which says nothing about
which assumption failed.

Use the assert feature to state these at the point they must hold.
Cover four kinds: lifecycle order, the fx:id fields that FXML fills in,
null contracts between collaborating classes, and postconditions such
as a list growing by exactly one when a task is added.

The fx:id assertions earn their place in particular. Nothing checks
that a Java field still matches an id in an XML file, so renaming one
leaves a null field that only fails later.

Leave input validation alone. A task number out of range or a deadline
missing /by is the user being human, not a broken assumption, and both
are already answered with a message. Asserting on them would crash
under -ea and check nothing without it.

Enable -ea through applicationDefaultJvmArgs, since the JVM ignores
every assert statement unless asked not to.

commitResults.messageTitle: Extract command handlers out of execute
commitResults.messageBody:
The execute method mixes two levels of abstraction. Some branches are a
single delegating call, such as returning the task list, while mark,
delete and todo reach into the list and the parser and do three steps
inline. A reader scanning for the set of commands Bucket understands
has to step over that detail, and at 41 lines the method had grown
past what fits in one screenful.

Move the multi-step branches into addTodo, markTask, findTasks and
deleteTask, so every branch of execute is a single call. The method now
reads as the list of commands and nothing else, while each handler
stays at one level. execute drops to 29 lines and the new handlers are
four to six each.

This is a pure restructuring. No behaviour changes: every reply and
error message is unchanged.
Extract command handlers out of execute

commitResults.messageTitle: Sort tasks by date when listing them
commitResults.messageBody:
Tasks are shown in the order they were added, so a deadline due next
year can sit above one due tomorrow. With more than a handful of tasks
the list stops being useful for working out what is next.

Order the list by date whenever it is shown, earliest first. Each kind
of task reports its own sort date: a deadline gives its due date, an
event gives its start date since that is when the user needs to be
somewhere, and a todo has no date at all and returns nothing. Sorting
therefore never asks what type a task is, which keeps the comparator
free of instanceof chains and leaves each type's rule beside the type.

Undated todos collect at the end. The sort is stable, so tasks sharing
a date, and the todos among themselves, stay in the order they were
added rather than being shuffled on every list.

Sort the stored list rather than a copy of it. The numbers shown come
from each task's position and mark and delete resolve a number back to
that same position, so ordering only the displayed text would make
"mark 2" act on a different task from the one printed as 2.

commitResults.messageTitle: Make the GUI asymmetric and resizable
commitResults.messageBody:
The two sides of the conversation looked alike: same bubble, same font,
and a large picture each, mirrored left and right. That reads as two
people talking when it is really a person and a tool. Errors looked
like every other reply, so a refused command was easy to miss. And the
window could not be resized, since the layout pinned its own size.

Give each side the treatment its content wants. Bucket's replies run
wide and left in a fixed-width font, because they are mostly task lists
whose columns need to line up. What the user typed is echoed as a short
right-aligned chip in a proportional font, and loses its picture: the
user knows who they are, and that width is better spent on the replies.

Carry the fact that a reply is an error alongside its text, in a new
Response record, so the GUI can tint those and mark them with a bar
down the left edge. Matching on the word OOPS!!! would instead have
tied presentation to wording.

Lay the window out as a transcript above an input bar rather than as
pinned coordinates, so it can be dragged to any size and the content
reflows. Move colours, fonts and spacing into a stylesheet, shrink the
remaining picture and clip it to a circle, and delete the user picture
now that nothing refers to it.
